label: In-school practice
disclaimer: These are in-school practice items to review methods from class. They do not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars.

items.title: Two main parts of a portfolio
items.question: Form 4 introductory lessons described two main parts of an SBA portfolio. What are they?
options: A PE log and a music test
Real exam-paper wording and high-score exemplars
A research workbook, and artwork / critical studies
School admin steps and the year calendar
items.explain: Lessons only teach portfolio structure: the research workbook runs through the process, and artwork / critical studies present the outcome.

items.title: What to observe first when drawing from life
items.question: In a life-drawing or observation exercise, what is most worth noticing first?
options: Whether you can copy a photo exactly in one go
Whether a real exam paper asks for this method
Whether you can skip looking and go straight to colour
Shape, proportion, and how the composition fits together
items.explain: Life drawing starts with looking: shape, proportion and composition, then you test media.

items.title: What a visual diary helps you do
items.question: What does a weekly visual diary mainly help you do?
options: Build a streak and keep a flame going
Record observations and slowly develop a theme
Copy wording from a real exam paper
Replace the teacher’s official mark
items.explain: A visual diary is a classroom record for observation and theme-building, not a streak game.

items.title: What to bring back from artist research
items.question: When you research an artist, what is most worth bringing back to your own theme?
options: Only pasting pictures, with no note about what you see
Copying whole sentences from a high-score exemplar
The methods they use, and how those methods connect to your own theme
Memorising the artist’s biography word for word
items.explain: Research needs interpretation and a turn back into your own making, not pictures alone.

items.title: What to ask when looking at earlier art
items.question: When looking at introductory examples of earlier Western or Chinese art, what is sound to ask together?
options: Whether it can be treated as a real exam model answer
What mark the maker scored at the time
Only the date, with no need to look further
Form, function, and cultural context
items.explain: Introductory looking asks about form, function and context, and does not treat the work as an exam answer.

items.title: How to use the three theme seeds
items.question: What do the three theme seeds “self, relationship, story” mainly help you do?
options: Force you to copy a particular real exam paper
Narrow your focus and develop a theme that belongs to you
Replace the research workbook
Compare the class to see whose theme is stronger
items.explain: Theme seeds help you narrow and develop a personal direction. They are not a contest or an exam bank.

items.title: What the exam-practice studio practises
items.question: In the exam-practice studio unit, what do lessons actually practise?
options: Memorising the wording of a real exam paper
Copying a high-score student exemplar
How to present a theme visually, and how to structure critical writing
Predicting an official public-exam score
items.explain: The exam-practice studio practises structure and method only. It does not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars.

items.title: Write about an image in three short parts
items.question: Choose an image you have seen in class, or a sketch of your own. Write three short parts: what you see; how you understand it; and what evidence you are using. Method only — do not copy a real exam paper.
items.hint: Two to four sentences in each part is enough. If you have no image to hand, write about a work discussed in class, and do not invent details you cannot see.

items.title: Choose one theme seed and write the next step
items.question: Choose one of “self, relationship, story”. Write how you would gather material in class, and what you want to try next. Keep all of it as classroom practice.
items.hint: You may mention interviews, sketches, photos or collected objects, and keep all of it as classroom practice.

items.title: Write your theme motive now
items.question: In two sentences, write your theme motive now: what do you care about, and why does it matter to you? If the theme is not fixed yet, write the one thing you most want to make clear.
items.hint: Axis: theme clarity. A concrete sentence is more useful than a list of keywords.

items.title: Write about material you have used
items.question: Note one piece of material you observed or recorded yourself, and one second-hand source you looked at. In one sentence each, say how it helps your current theme.
items.hint: Axis: research depth. A second-hand source can be a book, class material or a trusted webpage. Do not write a school name.

items.title: Write about one experiment and what you learned
items.question: Describe one media or technique experiment that did not go as expected. What did you do? What did you learn? What would you try next?
items.hint: Axis: media and technique experiments. A record of what did not work is still useful.

items.title: Write three steps you have changed
items.question: From your first composition to now, write three steps you have changed. For each step, note the problem you saw and how you changed it.
items.hint: Axis: completeness of process record. Skipping steps, or showing only the finished piece, makes progress harder to see.

items.title: Write a problem, a method, and a next step
items.question: Write one problem you noticed, one method you tried, and one step you want to try next time.
items.hint: Axis: reflection and learning progress. A grounded note is more useful than a slogan.

items.title: Write how one page or work carries the theme
items.question: Choose one workbook page or one work in progress. Write what a reader would notice first, and how that arrangement helps the theme come across.
items.hint: Axis: visual expression and structure. You may mention hierarchy, space, or how image and words work together. You do not need to claim the work is finished.
